Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Angola predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording (e.g., consultations, vaccinations, treatments). revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Angola record patient data (consultations, vaccinations, treatments) using paper-based registers at the point of care. The Ministry of Health has run the DHIS2 platform nationally since 2015, but this operates at the aggregation level: paper records from clinics are compiled and entered into DHIS2 at municipal or provincial offices, not digitised at the facility itself. Electronic medical record pilots, such as one for tuberculosis surveillance, are confined to a small number of urban facilities in Luanda and have not been extended to rural clinics. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet access, staff shortages, and limited IT training in rural areas.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No evidence found of digital case management or record-keeping in rural Angola police stations despite extensive searches. SIC offers online complaints, but core functions like incident reports and case files appear paper-based per standard African practices (e.g., signing physical documents warned in UK FCDO Prisoner Pack). US State Dept 2024 HR report details arrests, interrogations at stations, pretrial detention without digital mentions, indicating manual processes (US State Dept 2024 HR Angola). Justice digitization limited to ombudsman courts, not police (UNDP Angola). Rural areas likely paper-only given infrastructure challenges.

Recent government investment in policing technology, including new command-and-control centres with CCTV and vehicle-tracking capability, is concentrated in Luanda's urban municipalities and does not extend to rural record-keeping.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Angola predominantly use paper-based recording for attendance, enrollment, grades, and admin data, aggregated later into central EMIS/SIGE systems at provincial/district levels via paper forms or manual entry. Evidence: 2007 World Bank report describes initial school mapping exercise as first step to EMIS, implying manual collection (World Bank ICT Report). Recent GPE analyses highlight 'data and evidence' as high priority due to lack of timely data, indicating incomplete digitisation at facility level (GPE Angola Compact). No evidence of direct digital entry in rural schools; infrastructure poor—no electricity policies for schools, low ICT access (Education Profiles). SIGE systems exist but provincial/pilot scale, not rural-wide digital recording. Pilots and donor projects (e.g., Escola Meu Kamba) exist but limited.

A provincial initiative in Uige is beginning to equip around 100 of a planned 700-plus schools with computers and a school management system to digitise administrative processes that were previously handled manually, but this remains a limited, single-province pilot rather than a national standard. Poor rural electricity supply and low ICT access continue to constrain facility-level digitisation more broadly.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Angola predominantly use paper-based processes for birth registration, with forms filled manually at point of service and later digitized at higher levels. A 2023 UNECA survey self-reports Angola among 10 countries where all civil registration offices countrywide have digitized databases and electronic entry of vital events, with electronic transmission from local to central levels.UNECA CRVS Digitalization Report However, an African Union CRVS status report scores Angola's digitization as <35% (very weak), indicating limited electronic capture at local offices.AU CRVS Status Report UNICEF is procuring a CRVS assessment (2025), signaling ongoing gaps. Recent initiatives like 'Born with a birth certificate' target rural areas with ID issuance at hospitals (pilots in Zaire province), but routine rural registration remains paper-default. Barriers: poor rural infrastructure, electricity/internet gaps, low capacity; national digital ambitions (e.g., integrated platforms) outpace rural rollout, with coverage ~30% for IDs. Score 2 reflects self-claimed national digital but weak evidence for majority rural point-of-service use vs. aggregation-level digitization.

revision_notes: Original UNECA/AU sources reviewed. Fetched a 2021 IDRC/UNECA CRVS country snapshot for Angola, based on a Ministry of Justice and Human Rights questionnaire, which gives a more specific and authoritative picture than the aggregate national percentages previously cited: it explicitly distinguishes urban centres (computerised) from rural areas, which it describes as lacking civil registration infrastructure altogether, with paper registration books used and digitised only 'for further digitization' at a higher level. Also found 2024-2026 Angop press reporting on the World Bank-financed 'Njila' governance project, which has been rehabilitating and equipping birth registration posts with computer equipment across several provinces (including Bie and Huambo) since 2023, with some posts reported operational from August 2025. Weighing the 2021 baseline (rural = entirely paper at the point of registration) against the ongoing but partial 2023-2025 equipment rollout, score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed as the best current characterisation of a genuine but incomplete transition.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Angola have historically relied on paper registration books, with records digitised only when aggregated at a higher administrative level rather than captured electronically at the point of registration; a 2021 CRVS system assessment coordinated with the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights specifically noted the absence of civil registration infrastructure and continued reliance on paper books in rural areas. Since 2023, the World Bank-financed 'Njila' governance project has been rehabilitating and equipping birth registration posts with computer equipment across several provinces, including Bie and Huambo, with some posts becoming operational from August 2025, mostly at maternal and child health centres. This points to an ongoing but partial transition, with a growing number of rural registry posts gaining digital capability while most still depend primarily on paper-based processes.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Burundi has implemented DHIS2 nationally up to CDS (district) level for health data aggregation and analysis, enabling decision-making and improved outcomes DHIS2 Implementation History. Prior to digital projects in hospitals (2015+), systems were largely paper-based, including patient records and registers Hospital Information System Study. EMRs like OpenClinic GA piloted in 11 hospitals (mostly district level), but no evidence of widespread individual digital recording in rural primary clinics (health centers level 1-3). Rural clinics likely use paper registers/patient records, with aggregates compiled and entered into DHIS2 at district level, consistent with common African HMIS where facility-level is paper and higher levels digitize. No SARA/WHO assessment found confirming digital tools in rural facilities; digital pilots focus on reminders/mobile for specific programs, not core records.

A national workshop in April 2026 confirmed that Burundi's digital health tools (DHIS2, SIDAInfo, OpenClinic) remain fragmented and siloed, with facility-level data capture still predominantly manual. Aggregated indicators are compiled from paper registers into DHIS2 at district level, consistent with common regional practice, but individual-level digital recording at the rural clinic point of care is not evidenced.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Burundi's rural police stations record case files, complaints, and incident reports using handwritten paper procès-verbaux (PVs), as mandated by the Criminal Procedure Code (Articles 3-5, 61). PVs require physical signatures, page initials, oaths, and manual transmission to prosecutors; no digital methods mentioned. HRW 2010 report confirms rural OPJs rely on paper dossiers, lacking even basic paper supplies (donated by NGOs), vehicles, or comms; files physically transferred, often incomplete. Recent US State Dept HR reports (2023-2024) describe manual processes (e.g., magistrates failing to convene hearings due to backlogs, lost files), implying paper persistence. No evidence of digital case management systems at stations; general admin digitisation (e.g., voter registers, data protection law 2026) does not extend to rural police recording. Rural facilities (limited staffing, resources) predominantly/entirely paper-based, per francophone Africa norms (handwritten PVs standard).

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Burundi, known as communal état civil bureaus, record births using entirely paper-based processes: parents declare births within 15 days, presenting hospital notifications; officials assign volume numbers, stamp documents, and type extracts manually. No electronic data entry or databases at point-of-service.ECOI.net report based on Burundi Embassy A 2023 UNECA survey (Oct 2022-Apr 2023) confirms Burundi has no national electronic CRVS database, with business processes (notification to certification) remaining paper-based nationwide, including rural areas; records transferred via paper copies.UNECA-AfDB-COMESA CRVS Digitalization report No evidence of e-CRVS pilots, digital tools, or deployments in rural registries found in recent searches (up to 2026). Barriers include lacking IT infrastructure, electricity/internet in rural zones, understaffing, and funding shortages noted in regional CRVS assessments. While national digital economy diagnostics highlight ambitions,World Bank Burundi Digital Economy rural CRVS reality lags, with completeness rates low (implied by surveys) and no shift from manual recording.

revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices (communal état civil bureaus) in Burundi record births, deaths and marriages through an entirely paper-based process: parents present hospital birth notifications, officials assign volume numbers and stamp documents by hand, with no electronic data entry at the point of service. As of May 2026, the Ministry of the Interior had presented a new national digital civil registration and biometric ID platform, but this required legal amendments to the Family Code (which still mandates manual registration), remained subject to a pending implementing decree, and continued to face rural electricity and internet constraints (national internet penetration stood at 11.1% at end-2025). A parallel commune-level digitisation pilot supported by UNDP exists in Gitega, the country's second-largest urban centre, but no evidence indicates rural registry offices have moved to digital data capture. The US Social Security Administration confirms Burundi still has no single nationwide repository of civil registration records, which continue to be held locally.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Burundi predominantly use paper-based registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Data is collected manually at the school level and aggregated into a national Education Management Information System (EMIS), which includes annual statistical yearbooks published by the Ministry of Education (latest 2020-2021) UNESCO IICBA. EMIS has been operational since 2008 but faces data management challenges, with no evidence of routine digital entry at rural point-of-service. Digital systems are limited to isolated donor-funded pilots, such as Ideas Box offline digital libraries in 20 remote schools (2023, EU-funded) Libraries Without Borders and proposed ICT labs in 15 provinces (2022 NGO project). Key barriers include lack of electricity (only 15% rural access, 10% schools powered), teacher training gaps, poverty, and infrastructure deficits. National policies promote ICT integration since 2014, but rural reality lags, with data likely transcribed centrally rather than captured digitally on-site.

A more authoritative, dated 2024 Global Partnership for Education assessment states explicitly that 'data collection is paper-based at the school level, and electronic data entry is conducted at the central level' for Burundi's EMIS, directly confirming the existing code. A June 2026 AU-IPED workshop is helping Burundi self-assess and strengthen its EMIS but represents forward planning, not current facility-level digitisation. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed and dated to the 2024 GPE assessment, the most specific and current authoritative statement on facility-level data capture.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Burundi record attendance, enrolment and learning outcome data on paper at the school level; a 2024 Global Partnership for Education assessment confirms that 'data collection is paper-based at the school level, and electronic data entry is conducted at the central level' within the national Education Management Information System (EMIS), which is managed by the Ministry of National Education and Scientific Research and produces annual statistical yearbooks. Isolated donor-funded initiatives exist, such as offline 'Ideas Cube' digital libraries installed in around 20 remote schools from 2023, but these provide teaching content rather than digitising administrative or attendance records at source. A 2026 African Union-supported self-assessment of the EMIS against continental norms and standards is under way to identify improvements, but rural point-of-service data capture remains manual.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Benin predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data. Evidence from multiple sources indicates reliance on paper registers: Abt Global's PSHPA project distributed 4,000 health data registers to private facilities across all regions, implying manual entry before aggregation into DHIS2; a 2024 study in rural Bopa district references annual statistical reports and monthly data from health centers without digital mention; Enabel equipped 244 facilities (unspecified if rural) with IT for data collection, but not point-of-care patient records. National DHIS2 is used for aggregate reporting from district level, with high concordance to facility registers in some areas, suggesting paper at clinics transcribed upward. Pilots exist (e.g., some direct DHIS2 entry in one clinic, District.Team for management), but no evidence of majority rural point-of-service digital use. Barriers: poor infrastructure (power, internet), low ICT skills, funding gaps. National eHealth strategy (2017) aims for digital HIS, but rural reality lags, with paper default and digital limited to aggregation/pilots. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural clinics.

National DHIS2 use is confined to district-level aggregation and to a small number of urban facilities (for example Minonkpo Clinic in Cotonou) that enter data directly; the wider USAID-funded PSHPA project instead distributed 4,000 paper health registers to private facilities nationwide for later transcription upward. As of March 2025, a digital surveillance and teledermatology tool for neglected tropical diseases remains at pilot stage in three departments (Zou, Ouémé, Plateau) and has not been deployed at facility level. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet access and limited ICT skills among rural health staff. Overall, rural clinics capture patient data on paper, with digitisation occurring only at district aggregation level or in isolated urban/pilot sites.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Benin predominantly use paper-based systems for recording attendance (call registers), administrative data, and monitoring, as evidenced by NGO projects like AGIR in Atacora/Atlantic using paper absence tracking sheets filled weekly from registers Action Education. National EMIS exists, with INFRE producing statistical yearbooks from EMIS data focused on primary education UNESCO IICBA, but no evidence of digital entry at rural school level—likely paper collection aggregated upward. Electricity access in primary schools is only 35% (2021, up from 20% in 2016), below SSA average, with rural national access at 12% IMF. Most primary schools lack computers, especially public/rural ones, leading to low ICT literacy Southern Voice. Isolated pilots (e.g., mobile money fees in one rural secondary) do not indicate widespread PoS digitalisation. Key barriers: infrastructure deficits, poverty, low skills. National policies promote free primary education and ICT integration ambitions, but rural PoS remains paper-based, with digital at higher aggregation levels only.

revision_notes: Cited sources (UNESCO IICBA, Southern Voice, Action Education, IMF) fetched and verified; they support low rural school connectivity/computer access but do not address the national EducMaster platform. Fresh search found EducMaster/SIGE (the primary/maternelle sub-sector platform, in service for roughly three years) requires all school directors nationwide, not only urban ones, to register and continuously update learner and staff records directly on the platform, with a February 2026 ministerial directive threatening sanctions for non-compliant directors including in rural circonscriptions. This is facility-level digital administrative data capture not reflected in the original score of 1 (Entirely paper). Recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital): classroom/attendance recording remains paper-based while enrolment and staff data capture is now digital at facility level, notwithstanding rural infrastructure constraints (electricity, computers) that may require directors to use circonscription or personal devices to comply.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Benin now combine paper-based classroom practice with mandatory digital administrative record-keeping. School directors nationwide, including in rural areas, are required to register and continuously update learner enrolment, class lists and teaching-staff records directly on the government's EducMaster/SIGE platform, which underpins national statistics, the primary-leaving certificate (CEP) process and payroll oversight; a ministerial directive of February 2026 threatens sanctions against directors, including in rural circonscriptions, who fail to keep class-level data current on the platform. Day-to-day classroom activity, such as attendance call registers and in-class monitoring, continues to rely on paper tools, as illustrated by NGO-supported paper absence-tracking sheets used in Atacora and Atlantique. Electricity access in primary schools nationally was around 35% in 2021 (about 12% in rural areas), and most rural schools lack computers, so data entry onto EducMaster by rural directors is often constrained by infrastructure and may in practice depend on periodic access to a circonscription office or a personal device. Rural primary schools therefore operate a mixed model: routine classroom recording remains paper-based, while core administrative and enrolment data capture is digital.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Benin are transitioning from paper-based to hybrid systems. Traditional practice involves paper declaration vouchers completed at health centres or via village chiefs, entered into paper registers at municipal civil status offices. However, significant digitalisation is underway: the e-SIRCEV electronic civil registration system was deployed to 121 out of 164 registries by 2021. In October 2024, Benin received 2,050 mobile registration terminals from the World Bank/WURI project to enable digital birth registration directly into the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) and National Register of Civil Status Events (RNEC) at health facilities across all districts. In August 2025, ANIP launched a one-stop digital birth registration pilot in 10 health facilities including regional hospitals in Natitingou and Djougou, with data going directly into the RNPP and automatic PIN generation. By 2025, ANIP issued 10.5 million civil status and identity documents, with 75% of all identification procedures handled through digital channels (37% web portal, 30% mobile app, 8% USSD). However, ANIP itself acknowledges that rural areas remain underserved and are a priority for 2026. The initial point-of-service capture at rural registry offices still largely involves paper forms before digital entry, though the infrastructure for digital-first registration is rapidly expanding. UNECA rates Benin's CRVS digitisation below 35%.

Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed, as the evidence continues to describe a transitional, not yet generalised, rural rollout; no promotion to a higher code is warranted until the pilot is confirmed generalised to rural registry offices.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Benin operate a hybrid model that is still transitioning from paper to digital point-of-service registration. Traditional practice records births via paper declaration vouchers completed at health centres or through village chiefs before entry into paper municipal registers, and the e-SIRCEV electronic system had reached 121 of 164 registries by 2021. Since October 2024 the WURI-Benin project has distributed 2,050 mobile registration terminals to health facilities across all districts to enable direct digital entry into the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) and Register of Civil Status Events (RNEC), and in August 2025 the National Identification Agency (ANIP), with UNICEF and WURI support, launched a six-month one-stop-shop pilot in ten public health facilities, including regional and zone hospitals serving rural catchment areas such as Natitingou, Djougou and Borgou-Alibori, under which parents receive their child's Personal Identification Number by SMS without needing to visit the town hall. By early 2026, ANIP reported that 75% of all identification and civil status procedures nationally were conducted through digital channels (web portal, mobile app, USSD), with 10.5 million documents issued in 2025, though the agency continues to describe rural areas as underserved and has named them a priority for 2026 once the pilot is generalised. Point-of-service capture at most rural registry offices therefore still typically begins on paper, even as digital-first registration infrastructure expands rapidly around them.

Key barriers include unreliable electricity and internet at rural health posts, low digital literacy, heavy workloads creating dual paper-digital reporting burdens, and staff turnover. The scale of eCHIS deployment (~45% of health posts) represents meaningful digital presence at point of service, moving beyond entirely paper-based, though paper remains the predominant method.

Key barriers: poor accessibility (centers often >5km from villages), untrained volunteer staff, lack of electricity/connectivity, large backlog (>25% unregistered births). National CRVS Reform Strategy (2018-2022) aims at modernization/DHIS2 linkage, but rural point-of-service remains paper-dominant, with digital limited to aggregation/pilots—not shifting majority to digital recording.

Comments: Rural police stations in Liberia record criminal cases and complaints using paper files and dockets. A January 2026 report on Nyehn Town Police Station in rural Todee District describes no computers available; officers prioritize protecting paper documents from rain over duties, indicating entirely manual processes amid dilapidated infrastructure lacking basic logistics.FrontPageAfrica An EGAP study on rural community policing (2010s) notes historically low formal reporting (2% of crimes to police), relying on administrative data without digital mention.EGAP Digital systems exist at national/urban levels: UNDP-supported CSIS (2021, Montserrado urban pilot) uses tablets for biodata/GPS input and online aggregation, replacing paper stats reporting.UNDP CSIS CMIS/DHIS2 (2022 rollout to police) offers offline mobile app for case stats with GPS, improving data integrity, but no evidence of routine rural point-of-service use; training focused on county-level staff.UNDP CMIS Barriers: poor infrastructure/electricity, low connectivity, training gaps, resource scarcity in rural areas. National digital ambitions (UNDP pilots) contrast sharply with rural paper reality; systems likely for aggregate reporting post-paper collection. Score 1: entirely paper at rural facilities; digital limited to urban pilots.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Liberia record cases, complaints and crime statistics almost entirely on paper. A January 2026 report on the Nyehn Town Police Station in rural Todee District, Lower Montserrado County, describes a dilapidated facility with no computers available, where officers prioritise protecting paper case files from rain damage over other duties. UNDP-supported digital case management tools - an online Case Management Information System for justice institutions and a Crime Statistics Information System using tablets with GPS-tagged reporting - have been piloted since 2021-2022, but rollout has concentrated on Montserrado County and county-level training rather than routine use at rural stations. Persistent barriers include poor infrastructure, unreliable electricity and connectivity, and limited resources in rural areas.

Comments: Rural primary schools in Liberia predominantly use paper-based registers for daily administrative data, attendance, and learning records. Fresh evidence confirms code 2 is correct: the Ministry of Education's Geo-Mapping Monitoring and Evaluation System, launched March 2026 and piloted in five counties including rural Rivercess, Sinoe, Bomi and Gbarpolu, had schools input real-time, geo-referenced monitoring data directly on-site; June 2026 reporting confirms this pilot phase concluded with "encouraging results" and contributed to a rise in accredited schools nationwide. revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Liberia predominantly rely on paper-based registers for attendance, enrolment and administrative records, reflecting a national Education Management Information System still transitioning from a paper-based EMIS 1.0 to a digitised EMIS 2.0, hampered by funding shortfalls and weak ICT infrastructure. Some point-of-service digital data capture has now been demonstrated in rural areas, however: the Ministry of Education's Geo-Mapping Monitoring and Evaluation System, launched in March 2026 with a US$300,000 government investment, had school staff enter real-time, geo-referenced monitoring data directly on-site during its pilot phase across five counties, including rural Rivercess, Sinoe, Bomi and Gbarpolu. By June 2026 the pilot had concluded with positive results, feeding into a broader school accreditation and monitoring drive. A parallel 2025/2026 Annual School Census also introduced greater use of school-based data collection and digital validation, though this remains centred on County Data Hubs rather than direct facility-level digital entry. Overall, rural schools remain mostly paper-based with a growing but still limited degree of digital data capture.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices and civil registration points in Liberia predominantly use paper-based forms for birth registrations. The 15 county-level registration centers are located in urban districts, serving rural households located 5-10 km away (often requiring 5+ hours travel by foot). Completeness remains low at <25% as of 2018.UNECA CRVS Snapshot No computers in local registration or health facilities; paper records are standard, with data potentially aggregated digitally at county centers. Digital initiatives are limited to pilots and donor projects: The Mobile Birth Registration (MBR) pilot (2009-2012) used Nokia phones for data collection by district health officers in one rural county (Bomi), supplementing paper processes to enable certificate printing; it demonstrated feasibility but faced scale-up barriers and remained isolated.VTT ReportWHO eCRVS Review Recent UNICEF efforts (2024) integrate birth registration in 98% health districts using tablets/online systems linked to DHIS2 for digital certificates, but challenges like unreliable electricity, internet, resources, and decentralized accountability persist, indicating non-standardized use.FrontPageAfrica/UNICEF Key barriers: poor infrastructure/power, low capacity, post-conflict fragility. National plans (2016-2020) envision expansion and online rollout, but rural point-of-service remains paper-default with digital only in isolated health-linked pilots—not majority routine use. Score 2 fits: predominantly paper with some digital pilots.

revision_notes: Confirmed at 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), superseding the older 2011 mobile-registration pilot and 2018/2019 UNECA snapshot cited previously. UNICEF's December 2024 statement describes decentralisation of birth registration to all 15 counties and 98% of health districts, with tablets and an online registration system used for issuing digital birth certificates - a materially more advanced digital footprint than the earlier isolated pilots. However, an April 2026 CENTAL "Service-on-the-Wheel" mobile registration drive in rural Bong County reported technical difficulties limiting on-the-spot digital certificate printing, and standard process descriptions (World Bank ID4D) still show paper birth notification forms as the entry point, with data entered into an electronic database at a later stage rather than always at first point of contact. This mixed evidence supports "mostly paper - some digital" rather than a higher code.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry services in Liberia operate through a decentralised network of county-level registration centres and health-facility-linked registration points, with birth notification typically first recorded on paper before being entered into a central electronic database. Digitalisation has advanced since earlier isolated pilots: as of December 2024, UNICEF reported that birth registration had been decentralised to all 15 counties, reaching 98% of health districts, with tablets and an online registration system used to issue digital birth certificates, and records integrated into the DHIS2 platform for real-time reporting. In practice, however, digital delivery in rural areas remains uneven; an April 2026 mobile "Service-on-the-Wheel" registration drive in rural Bong County registered 477 children but encountered technical difficulties that delayed printing of digital certificates for many of them. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, and rural households often remain several hours' travel from a registration point. Overall, rural civil registry offices are best characterised as mostly paper-based with a growing but still partial degree of digital data capture.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics in Libya record patient data using paper-based systems, with aggregated data collated manually and reported upwards to district/national levels. No evidence of electronic medical records (EMR) or digital patient registration at point-of-service in rural facilities. A 2016 readiness study of five rural clinics found no e-health technologies in use and IT equipment not utilized for clinical purposes, rating maturity at level zero.University of Brighton Thesis. Recent assessments confirm national medical records remain paper-based, with no interoperable electronic health records.BMC Primary Care Assessment. DHIS2 adopted nationally in 2018 for monitoring/evaluation, piloted in limited PHC centers (e.g., 6 sites) and rolled out for aggregate reporting/surveillance, but not integrated into clinical care or point-of-care patient records; interviewees noted it is "too far removed from clinical care."WHO EMRO DHIS2 Training; WHO HIS 2017. Isolated donor projects like Speetar "Health Dots" e-clinics target rural south but remain pilots. Key barriers: protracted conflict damaging infrastructure (20% PHC facilities inaccessible/closed), electricity/internet shortages, lack of ICT/training, fragmented governance. National policy (2030 Vision, 2025-30 digital roadmap) aspires to digital HIS/electronic records, but rural reality lags with paper default and digital limited to upward aggregation/pilots—not PoS standard.

The 2024 BMC rapid mixed-methods assessment (peer-reviewed, government-commissioned) explicitly states that medical records remain paper-based and health management information systems are not in routine use at national or local level, and identifies the absence of interoperable EHRs as a critical weakness. The Brighton thesis (rural clinic e-health readiness study, five rural clinics) found no clinical ICT use, rating maturity at level zero. A November 2025 LibyaReview article confirms DHIS2 remains a regional reporting/surveillance tool under expansion discussion, not a point-of-care system. Small ICRC/Swiss TPH ALMANACH digital decision-support pilots (2023-24, ~25 PHCCs) do not appear to be rural-targeted or to change the general picture. revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Libya continue to rely on paper-based patient records at the point of care. A 2024 rapid mixed-methods assessment of Libya's primary care system confirms that medical records remain paper-based and that health management information systems are not in routine use at national or local level, with the absence of interoperable electronic health records identified as a critical weakness. A facility-level e-health readiness study of five rural clinics found no clinical use of ICT, rating maturity at the lowest level of the assessment framework. DHIS2 is being expanded nationally, with a further ministerial review in November 2025, but it functions as an aggregate reporting and surveillance tool fed from paper facility records rather than a point-of-care digital system, and pilot digital decision-support tools remain limited to a small number of donor-supported facilities. Data capture at rural clinics therefore remains entirely paper-based.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Libya's rural police stations record case files, complaints, and incident reports using paper-based procedures as per the 1953 Code of Criminal Procedure (still applicable). Judicial officers (police) draw up "reports" on incidents, seizures in sealed pouches, notifications, and monthly statistics submitted physically to prosecution; no mention of digital tools at station level. In remote areas, police delegated for felony investigations but refer to prosecution—implies paper transmission. No evidence found of digital case management systems deployed to rural stations; limited digital training for prosecutors/cybercrime urban-focused. Post-2011 instability fragmented policing; rural areas rely on local/customary resolution bypassing formal digital systems. General paper-based practice nationwide, score 1 per rules.

revision_notes: Fetched cited sources (DCAF Libyan Criminal Justice System database and USIP Policing Libya 2016) which confirm paper-based, prosecution-supervised evidence procedures under the still-applicable 1953 Code of Criminal Procedure, and a fragmented, conflict-affected policing structure, but neither speaks directly to rural police stations' record-digitisation status. A fresh search found no rural-specific evidence either way. Best available corroboration is indirect: a 2023 Libyan academic study (SEM survey of 205 Ministry of Interior employees) found e-management system adoption within the Ministry still at an early stage with infrastructure and staffing barriers, and an October 2023 LibyaReview report on digital transformation discussions for the Ministry of Interior cites ongoing digital-infrastructure and specialist-staffing challenges. The only concrete MoI digitisation initiatives found (a 2021 EU/UNDP Model Police Station pilot and a 2023 smart-surveillance camera pilot for traffic/licensing) are confined to Tripoli and unrelated to rural station record-keeping. Score of 1 is confirmed as the best-supported inference, but the evidence base is indirect and national-level rather than rural-facility-specific, so this is flagged for human review.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Libya continue to operate under paper-based case management procedures. The 1953 Code of Criminal Procedure, which remains the operative legal framework, prescribes paper reports, sealed evidence pouches and monthly statistical returns submitted physically to the Public Prosecution, with no digital equivalent specified for station-level record keeping. National-level assessments describe e-management system adoption within the Ministry of Interior as still at an early stage, constrained by weak digital infrastructure and a shortage of specialised staff, and the limited digital-transformation pilots identified (a smart surveillance camera trial and a single EU/UNDP-funded Model Police Station) are confined to Tripoli. No evidence of digital case-recording or record-management systems has been identified at rural police stations, which remain paper-based by default amid the post-2011 fragmentation of policing and reliance on customary dispute resolution in many rural areas.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Libya's Civil Registration Authority (CRA) operates 12 branches, 133 issuing offices, and 400 service offices covering all Libya, including rural areas, all fully automated and electronically linked via a single database since at least 2020, enabling high-quality timely data (100% birth registration, >90% deaths) Seha.ly 2020 report. UNFPA assessment shows computers used in compilation (79%), storage (68%), validation (63%), transmission (58%), with adequate peripheral infrastructure UNFPA Arab CRVS. Older UN paper (~1980s) describes paper triplicate forms at local level with central computerization UNStats, but recent sources confirm shift to digital. Recent mentions of electronic civil registry phases. Predominantly digital at rural facilities, some legacy paper possible.

revision_notes: Fetched all three cited sources plus a fresh search. The seha.ly 2020 report confirms the CRA's 12 branches, 133 issuing offices and 400 service offices nationwide, including rural areas, are linked via a single automated database. The 2022 UNFPA assessment, however, shows computer use across compilation, storage, validation and transmission stages ranging only from 58-79% (not full automation), indicating paper remains part of the workflow at many offices. This is confirmed by a September 2024 Libya Herald report on the CRA's 'Intilaqa' project, an ongoing exercise (begun around 2021, still underway in September 2024) to reconcile roughly 1.8 million Libyan family paper records (some untouched since the 1970s) against the electronic database, with 257 of the CRA's offices having completed matching/scanning by that date. This is strong, current evidence that substantial legacy paper records persist alongside the digital system, supporting the existing 'Mostly digital - some paper' rating rather than a promotion to 'Entirely digital'; no promotion is warranted.
revised_comments: Libya's Civil Registration Authority operates a single automated database linking its 12 branches, 133 issuing offices and 400 service offices across the country, including rural areas, enabling near-complete birth registration and high death-registration coverage. Facility-level data entry is substantially digital: an assessment found computers used at 58-79% of stages in the compilation, storage, validation and transmission of registration data. However, legacy paper archives remain significant: the CRA's 'Intilaqa' project, still underway as of September 2024, is reconciling around 1.8 million Libyan family paper records, some dating to the 1970s, against the electronic database, with 257 of its offices having completed matching and scanning. This combination of a largely digital core registration system alongside substantial ongoing paper-record reconciliation places rural civil registry offices at mostly digital with some paper, rather than entirely digital.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Lesotho continue to rely predominantly on paper-based recording, including Occurrence Books, custody logs and dockets, particularly where electricity and telecommunications are absent. Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: In rural primary healthcare clinics (health centers), patient data recording is predominantly paper-based for general care. Non-HIV/TB patients use paper health booklets, with data manually aggregated into national DHIS2 at higher levels MCC Blog 2023. For HIV/TB/PMTCT/cervical screening/pharmacy, eRegister EMR is deployed nationwide at all 170 government health centers (many rural) using decentralized local servers to handle poor connectivity/power; data auto-syncs to DHIS2 Oxford Digital Health 2024. Some duplicate paper processes persist. Digital systems are donor-driven (PEPFAR/ICAP) for specific diseases, not standard point-of-care for majority routine care. Pilots like village health worker tablets (BKM) exist but community-level. Barriers: unreliable power (outages, failing solar), low connectivity, technical capacity reliant on partners. MCC compact (2024+) plans expansion to all diseases, but currently not predominant at most rural clinics for all recording. Gap: National ambitions (Digital Health Strategy 2025-30 validated 2024) and HIV digital success contrast with paper-dominant routine rural PoC.

Fresh searches surfaced two 2025 peer-reviewed studies: a May 2025 cross-sectional study of eRegister use in Mafeteng district (17 facilities) confirming generally positive uptake but persistent electricity/connectivity barriers, and a November 2025 qualitative study confirming the eRegister covers five specific programmes and that government intends to phase out paper recording only once eRegister is fully operational nationwide - i.e. not yet the case. Code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed with more current sourcing.
revised_comments: Routine patient data recording in Lesotho's rural primary healthcare clinics remains predominantly paper-based, with paper health booklets used for most general care and data manually aggregated into DHIS2 at higher levels. For HIV, TB, antenatal and cervical-screening services, an electronic register (eRegister, built on the Bahmni platform) is deployed across more than 170 government health facilities nationwide, including many rural sites, using decentralised local servers to cope with unreliable power and connectivity, with data automatically synchronised to DHIS2. Studies from 2025 describe generally positive healthcare-worker perceptions of the eRegister but confirm that network connectivity and electricity outages remain significant operational barriers, and that the government envisages paper-based recording being phased out only once the eRegister is fully operational nationwide. Routine point-of-care recording for the majority of rural clinic services therefore remains paper-based alongside disease-specific digital systems.

Gap: National electronic aggregation ambition vs. paper-default at most ~10,000 rural points; pilots cover minority of facilities, fitting score 2.

revised_comments: Civil registration in Lesotho's rural areas is predominantly paper-based, delivered through outreach by Civil Registration Officers and, since 2020, through deployment at health facilities and community councils. The Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation and UNICEF signed a 2026 work plan to continue developing a MOSIP-based digital identity ecosystem linked to civil registration, indicating that national-level digitalisation remains a work in progress rather than complete.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Mozambique primarily use paper-based methods for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Core EMIS data is collected via hand-filled standardized paper questionnaires during semi-annual school censuses (enrolment in March, results in December), covering student numbers, repeaters, teachers, infrastructure, and resources. These forms are forwarded through districts to provinces for collation and centralized digitization in Maputo—no digital entry at school level. Attendance and marks are tracked in handwritten 'livro de turma' class registers, forming the basis for semester/annual paper school reports on staffing, finances, and pedagogy, which have limited integration with EMIS. No evidence found of routine electronic recording at point-of-service in rural schools. Digital pilots exist, e.g., Carta Escolar (GIS for school mapping/planning, piloted in some provinces but not fully functional or used for attendance/learning data); limited ICT initiatives focus on secondary/urban schools or learning (e.g., SchoolNet, NEPAD e-Schools demos), not admin recording. Key barriers: lack of electricity, computers, internet in rural areas; untrained staff; unreliable infrastructure; focus on basic operations. National EMIS provides aggregate planning data, but rural reality remains paper-dominant, with digitization only at higher levels—wide gap between policy ambitions and rural implementation. National digital ambitions (e.g., drone training, cyber units) contrast sharply with rural paper reality, where mobiles aid reporting but core docket recording remains manual.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Malawi predominantly use paper-based systems for patient data recording at point-of-care. Health Passports (HPs), patient-held paper booklets, are updated manually during consultations with symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, and plans; they serve as the primary medical record since most rural facilities do not maintain outpatient files on-site. Post-consultation, data clerks transcribe from HPs into paper facility registers (e.g., OPD), which are aggregated monthly and entered into DHIS2 at district level—not at the facility POC. Digital initiatives like openSRP e-register (tablet-based EHR) are limited to pilots (e.g., Bilira Health Centre since ~2021, covering thousands of patients but one site) and community tools like iCHIS (3 districts). EHRs are mainly in urban/central hospitals. Key barriers: poor handwriting/abbreviations in HPs, low literacy, resource shortages (power/internet), high workload, no standardization/training. National policy (e.g., Digital Health Strategy) aims for digital HIS, DHIS2 mobile allows some facility entry (41% facilities use digital tech), but rural POC remains paper-default with digital for aggregate reporting only—gap between ambition and reality.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools

revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Eswatini have historically recorded enrolment, attendance and learner data on paper, submitted through instruments such as the Annual Education Census for later manual entry into central systems. Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Seychelles (e.g., Praslin, La Digue, Mont Fleuri) record criminal cases and complaints using a national digital case management system built on FileMaker platform, funded by UNODC and developed by Transmedia. Deployed across all stations, which are connected nationwide, allowing point-of-service entry of incident reports, occurrence books, and case details on desktops/iPads. It replaced parallel manual records, digitizes intake forms, enables searches across districts, cross-references (vehicles, phones), and supports court use. Detective from Mont Fleuri station (Mahe rural-ish) confirms: "all police stations are connected... transformed the life of the Seychelles police force." Evolutions include 2023 Cautions module, digitized Occurrence Book. Some paper may linger for minor/admin tasks, but digital is standard at rural point-of-service. No evidence of majority paper or pilots only. Barriers: small population (98k), remote islands may limit infra/maintenance, but connectivity confirmed. National e-gov push aligns with rural reality.Winsoft International; Seychelles Police; Forensic Science Int.

Some manual documentation likely persists alongside the digital system, for example handwritten statements taken at first point of contact, consistent with a predominantly digital but not fully paperless environment at rural stations.

Comments: Seychelles Ministry of Education operates a national EMIS for collecting school data on students, staff, infrastructure from all institutions, including primary schools on outer islands (rural equivalents). Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Seychelles (termed community health centres or PHCs on outer islands/districts) continue to rely predominantly on paper-based patient data recording, despite national eHIS rollout. The Ministry of Health's 2022-2026 Strategic Plan states data capture is "primarily paper-based" with duplicative tools, and eHIS implementation (started 2020) has stalled, creating an urgent need for transition Seychelles MoH Strategic Plan. The 2023 Annual Performance Report shows progress with 88% eHIS patient registration coverage in PHCs (up from 29% in 2022), but actual consultation recording lags, remaining below expectations even after EMR training for 140 doctors MoH Performance Report 2023. No specific rural/outer island distinctions, but given small scale (17 CHCs nationwide), rollout likely covers them. Digital systems like eHIS integrate surveillance/labs centrally, but point-of-care is hybrid. Barriers: stalled implementation, staff training/satisfaction, data quality. National ambition for full eHIS contrasts with persistent paper dominance at clinics Commonwealth WHO Assessment. Score 3 reflects majority digital registration standardizing, with paper fallback for consultations.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Chad predominantly use paper registers for patient data recording at the point of service. Aggregate data from these paper records is collated monthly and forwarded to district levels, where it is entered digitally into DHIS2, with 96% of districts now reporting directly into the system as of 2022.DHIS2 Chad transition. A 2021 study in Massaguet district (including rural health centres) confirmed routine use of paper-based external consultation registers and HMIS forms, with data digitized only at district level using Excel; no EMR at clinics, and paper stock-outs common, leading to inaccuracies.BMC study Massaguet. No evidence found of routine digital entry, EMR, or DHIS2 at point of care in rural clinics; plans exist for tablets in northern regions for offline DHIS2 aggregate entry, but not implemented widely.DHIS2 Chad transition. Key barriers: poor internet/power in rural north, staff workload, form stock-outs, low digital literacy. National ambition via DHIS2 rollout contrasts with rural paper reality; pilots/digital limited to aggregation, not point-of-service.

revision_notes: Original sources (DHIS2 transition note, 2021 Massaguet BMC study) were fetched and confirm paper-based registers with digitisation occurring only at district level, not at the clinic. A further search identified documented facility-level digital data capture: a tablet-based clinical decision support system (CDSS), piloted as SysRef from 2019 in three rural primary healthcare facilities in southern Chad and now operating as SANU-TD (Sante Numerique au Tchad), with health workers entering patient consultation data directly onto tablets at point of care (offline, synced later). A May 2024 Geneva Health Forum poster confirms the tool is being extended to the national health system in southern Chad under the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation-funded PADS programme. This is genuine facility-level digital capture, not just aggregation, though still confined to a subset of rural clinics in the south alongside the still-dominant paper-register system documented in Massaguet district and the DHIS2 rollout. revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Chad remain predominantly paper-based, with patient consultations recorded in paper registers and HMIS forms that are aggregated and entered electronically only at district level (DHIS2, with 96% of districts reporting directly as of 2022). Facility-level digital data capture nonetheless exists in a small but growing subset of rural clinics: a tablet-based clinical decision support system, piloted as SysRef (2019-2023) in three primary healthcare facilities in southern Chad and now operating as SANU-TD, enables health workers to record consultations digitally at the point of care, and the tool is being extended to the national health system in southern health districts under the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation-funded PADS programme. Barriers to wider digitisation include poor rural connectivity and power supply and low digital literacy, meaning paper remains the norm outside these pilot districts.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Evidence suggests rural police stations in Chad are still predominantly paper-based, with digitisation happening mainly at central level. INTERPOL's EU-funded Chad Police Information System (SIPT) (a WAPIS-like system) was created to move away from paper records and provide a centralized computerized database for police data (persons, offences, vehicles, documents), managed via a Data Collection/Registration Center (DACORE/CREDOP) that records and validates police data; INTERPOL notes longer-term plans to deploy access to the system across agencies and regions/border posts depending on infrastructure, implying that broad station-level digital entry is not yet universal. Recent US State Department human rights reporting describes police and detention procedures but does not indicate routine digital case/complaint recording, consistent with continued reliance on traditional paper proces-verbaux at station level, especially outside N'Djamena. Overall: predominantly paper at rural stations, with some digitalisation through SIPT at national/central nodes and potential roll-out pilots.

Legal and governance frameworks for the SIPT were only finalised in January 2024, and implementation has historically been delayed by political instability. There is no evidence that digital case recording extends to police stations outside the central DACORE, and traditional paper proces-verbaux continue to be used at station level, particularly outside N'Djamena.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Chad predominantly use paper-based systems for birth registration. Recent data shows only 26% national birth registration rate among under-5s, with 84% of children rural and significantly lower rates in rural vs urban areas (largest gaps in Chad per UAPS 2024 analysis), indicating poor coverage and likely manual recording at remote points. A UNICEF-supported Tasdjil digital app (launched 2022, offline-capable, <10 min process) has enabled 109k+ registrations, often at health facilities, representing a donor pilot to boost access. No evidence of majority rural facilities using digital point-of-service; paper remains default. Barriers: remoteness (Chad 80%+ rural), poverty, low awareness, infrastructure deficits. National efforts (e.g., centers, campaigns) exist but gap persists between policy and rural reality-digital limited to pilots, not scaled/standardized at rural registries. Score conservative due to thin specific evidence on recording methods.

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). The original UAPS abstract and UNICEF USA story were fetched and support the description of low overall birth registration with a UNICEF-backed digital pilot (Tasdjil). revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Chad rely predominantly on paper-based processes, reflected in a national birth registration rate of just 25.5% among under-fives (2019 MICS6), with a pronounced urban-rural gap (50% urban versus 21.1% rural) and death and marriage registration described as almost non-existent. Digitisation of civil status records is being piloted in a limited number of health districts in partnership with UNICEF, UNFPA and UNHCR, most visibly through the offline-capable Tasdjil mobile application (launched 2022), which has enabled over 109,000 birth registrations by linking registration to health facility visits, and through one-stop birth registration offices such as that opened in Bol, Lake Province, in November 2023. These initiatives represent meaningful but geographically limited pockets of digital capture; most rural registry points continue to depend on manual paper-based recording, and coverage remains low overall.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics in Togo predominantly use paper-based patient registers and records at point of care. Aggregated weekly surveillance data (e.g., cases/deaths for 15 diseases) is tallied from facility registries onto paper forms, then sent via SMS using the Argus app on dedicated phones for upward reporting—not patient-level digital entry Argus study. No evidence of routine EMR or DHIS2 at rural clinics; only 11.8% of surveyed doctors nationwide use EMR, reflecting low digitization Doctors EMR survey. Pilots exist: Integrate Health ICBHSS in 21 northern rural facilities focuses on clinical mentoring/supply chains without digital records ICBHSS protocol; DokitaEyes app (230 facilities) for digital patient files, but private/NGO-led, offline-capable, not standard public rural practice; recent World Bank $100M digital project connects facilities to broadband (2024), but focuses on connectivity/skills, not POC systems. National DHIS2 used for aggregate HMIS/IDSR, not facility-level recording. Barriers: poor internet/power in rural areas, low EMR adoption, reliance on paper transmission historically. Policy (e.g., National Digital Health Center) aims at digital transformation, but rural POC remains paper-based, with digital limited to pilots/aggregation. (198 words)

revision_notes: Cited sources (Argus study, ICBHSS protocol, World Bank release) were fetched and support a paper-based baseline, but a fast search surfaced fresher, authoritative evidence of programme-specific digital capture that the original comment omitted: SanteComTogo, a national electronic community health information system, launched March 2024 and has digitised (replacing paper) household registration and care-visit data for over 1,000 community health workers across six districts of the Maritime Region, scaling nationally since. A peer-reviewed 2025 article (Revue Africaine des Sciences Sociales et de la Sante Publique) independently confirms that DHIS2-based digitalisation of health data production has been replacing paper registers since 2021 for malaria chemoprevention and bed-net campaign data. DHIS2's own account of the EPI/immunisation package (since c.2015-2020) also documents decentralisation of data entry to facility level. This constitutes multiple, corroborating, fetched sources for at least partial facility/community-level digital capture, which the original code of 1 (entirely paper) does not reflect. Recalculated to 2 (mostly paper, some digital) rather than higher, as general clinical records and patient registers at most rural clinics remain paper-based and EMR use among doctors nationally is low (~12%).
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare data capture in Togo presents a mixed paper-digital picture rather than a wholly paper-based one. Since 2021, national malaria chemoprevention and bed-net distribution reporting, and since March 2024 the SanteComTogo electronic community health information system, have shifted specific data streams from paper registers to app-based digital capture; SanteComTogo alone covers over 1,000 community health workers across six districts of the Maritime Region at launch, with national scale-up under way. Facility-level immunisation (EPI) data entry via DHIS2 has similarly been decentralised to the facility level for some years. Nonetheless, general patient registration and clinical records at most rural clinics remain paper-based, electronic medical record use among doctors nationally is low (around 12%), and a $100 million World Bank programme approved in December 2024 to connect public institutions to broadband has yet to deliver facility-level point-of-care digital systems. Data capture in rural clinics is therefore best characterised as mostly paper with some digital elements.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Togo's rural policing is handled by Gendarmerie Nationale posts. The Criminal Procedure Code mandates officers (incl. rural gendarmerie) to draft and sign procès-verbaux (PVs) on-site for incidents, with physical custody registers requiring signatures—standard paper-based francophone practice [Togo Code de Procédure Pénale]. UK FCDO arrest guidance describes signed station registers and "police records" for inquiries, implying manual processes [UK Prisoner Pack]. Central WAPIS (2022) enables national data sharing but no evidence of initial rural recording being digital; likely paper first, digitized centrally (scores 1 per rules) [INTERPOL WAPIS]. No rural digital tools on official sites. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural facilities.

revision_notes: Cited sources were fetched; the Criminal Procedure Code and WAPIS material support the original paper-based assessment, but the UK FCDO prisoner pack is only weakly probative (it describes station registers generically, not specifically rural gendarmerie practice). A search for fresher evidence found that WAPIS/CIPT (operational since 2022) is a central national data-collection and analysis centre in Lomé rather than a rural point-of-capture system, confirming the original view that it does not establish digital recording at rural stations. However, a May 2024 UNDP press release describes a pilot providing computer equipment (14 desktops, printers, scanners) to three rural-region prosecutors' offices (Mandouri/Savanes, Pagouda/Kara, Tabligbo/Maritime) and six police/gendarmerie investigation units, as part of a project to interconnect prosecutors with police judiciaire units. This is suggestive but inconclusive evidence of emerging digitisation reaching rural units, and it is a single source describing a narrow pilot rather than confirmed digital data capture. In line with guidance not to upgrade on a single weak source, the code is kept at 1 (entirely paper), but the row is flagged for human review given this emerging, only partially corroborated evidence.
revised_comments: Rural policing in Togo is conducted mainly through Gendarmerie Nationale posts operating under the Code de Procedure Penale, which requires officers to draft and sign proces-verbaux and maintain physical custody registers on-site, a standard paper-based practice. The West Africa Police Information System (WAPIS), operational since 2022 through Togo's Centre d'Information Policiere in Lome, centralises criminal case data for national and regional sharing but operates at a central rather than rural facility level. A small UNDP-supported pilot in 2024 supplied computer equipment to a handful of rural-region prosecutors' offices and police/gendarmerie investigation units as part of a project to interconnect prosecutors with police judiciaire units, but there is no clear evidence yet that this has changed how case data is captured at the point of contact in rural stations. Data capture at rural police facilities is therefore assessed as entirely paper-based.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Togo's rural registry offices (état civil at prefectures/town halls) predominantly use paper-based recording. Births are declared at local Etat Civil with hospital attestation, recorded in multi-leaflet paper registers; leaflet given as Acte de Naissance. No electronic CRVS database; paper used throughout for transfers to central levels per ECA-APAI report. Low completeness (e.g., 22-30% late registrations via courts). Recent pilots (Dec 2025) allow online requests for copies in 5 communes (some rural like Avé 2), implying scanned paper records for digital access, but core recording at rural facilities remains paper/manual. Pilots indicate emerging digital services, but not at recording stage. Score 2: predominantly paper with some digital pilots.

revision_notes: The original row's Comments text concluded 'Score 2: predominantly paper with some digital pilots' yet the Value Code field recorded 1, an internal inconsistency. The cited sources were fetched and confirm a predominantly paper CRVS system with an emerging digital pilot for requesting copies of civil-status documents in five communes launched December 2025 (Agoe-Nyive 1, Golfe 1, Ave 2, Zio 2, Lacs 1). Further searching found this pilot has continued to develop: a UNDP-supported birth tele-declaration platform has operated in commune Golfe 3 since April 2024, delivering around 14,800 birth certificates in eight months, and in April 2026 the five pilot communes received computer equipment (desktops, printers, scanners) to support the digitisation drive, described by officials as an intermediate step before nationwide rollout. Per the metadata guidance that only facility-level data capture (not higher-level digitisation of already-recorded paper data) should count, the copy-request portal itself is not directly relevant, but the birth tele-declaration platform and the equipping of registry offices for digital processing indicate genuine, if limited, digital capture is beginning to reach rural civil registry offices. Recalculated to 2 (mostly paper, some digital), consistent with the original comment's stated conclusion and resolving the code/comment mismatch.
revised_comments: Civil registration in Togo's rural prefectures and communes remains predominantly paper-based, with births, deaths and marriages recorded in multi-leaflet paper registers at local etat civil offices and low completeness of late registrations (roughly a quarter of cases handled via the courts). Digitisation is nonetheless emerging: since April 2024 a UNDP-supported birth tele-declaration platform has operated in the commune of Golfe 3, delivering around 14,800 birth certificates in its first eight months; since December 2025 an online portal has allowed citizens in five pilot communes (Agoe-Nyive 1, Golfe 1, Ave 2, Zio 2 and Lacs 1) to request copies of civil-status documents and track processing in real time; and in April 2026 these pilot communes received computer equipment to support the digitisation drive, described by officials as an intermediate step ahead of nationwide rollout. This combination of largely paper-based recording with a small but growing set of digital pilots is best characterised as mostly paper with some digital.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Togo's rural primary schools use a hybrid paper-digital system for data collection (attendance, enrollment, grades). Data from 16,000 schools, including rural primaries, is first collected on paper forms at schools, then transmitted to district education inspections for review and subsequent digitization into StatEduc. Digital processing/analysis occurs via DHIS2 EMIS (piloted nationally since 2021 with GPE KIX/Norad support), but initial recording remains paper-based at facility level. No evidence of on-site digital recording in rural schools; digitization is at district level. This aligns with francophone African norms and recent reports (2022-2025). Score 1 as rural facilities record on paper.

revision_notes: All three cited sources were fetched and confirm the original assessment: data from the country's roughly 16,000 pre-primary, primary and secondary schools is first collected on paper forms at school level and only digitised once it reaches district inspectorates, where it is entered into StatEduc and then processed/visualised via a DHIS2-based EMIS operating at national scale since 2019. A further search did not find any evidence of on-site digital data capture in rural primary schools; digitisation consistently occurs only after forms leave the school. The original code of 1 (entirely paper) is confirmed, correcting only the year (previously blank) and minor detail (DHIS2/StatEduc integration dates to 2019 nationally, per DHIS2's own implementation page, rather than 2021 as stated in the original comment, which appears to refer to the GPE KIX-funded EMIS enhancement phase).
revised_comments: Togo's Ministry of Primary, Secondary and Technical Education relies on a hybrid paper-digital education management information system. Data from the country's roughly 16,000 pre-primary, primary and secondary schools is first collected on paper forms at the school level, then forwarded to district education inspectorates for entry into StatEduc, a statistical application used in some twenty countries. Since 2019, StatEduc has been complemented nationally by a DHIS2-based EMIS, developed with GPE KIX and Norad support, which processes and visualises the collected data through dashboards covering enrolment, teacher-pupil ratios and exam results, decentralising analysis to district and school actors. Because data capture at the school itself remains paper-based, with digitisation occurring only once forms reach the district level, rural primary schools are assessed as recording data entirely on paper.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Tunisia predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data, including nursing documentation, which remains largely manual across public facilities despite national eHealth initiatives. No evidence found of routine EMR or DHIS2 use at point-of-care in rural clinics; WHO data confirms no EHR in primary care facilities (clinics/health centers). Recent digital efforts focus on urban/regional hospitals (e.g., full digitalization target by 2026), telemedicine pilots, connectivity expansion to primary facilities, and national systems like "One Health," but these represent emerging donor/government projects not yet standard at rural point-of-service. A 2024 study notes paper-based nursing records cause traceability issues, with EMR gaining momentum but not implemented routinely. Barriers include poor internet in rural areas, staff training gaps, fragmented HIS, and focus on aggregation over facility-level digitization. National ambitions (e.g., 2025 digital hospital projects, World Bank support for EMR training) outpace rural reality, where paper registers prevail for patient encounters, with data likely transcribed later at district levels.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 confirmed. All three originally cited sources were fetched and support paper-based recording at rural primary-care level. A fresh search located a February 2025 statement from Tunisia's Minister of Health confirming that digitisation of the unified medical record has reached hospitals (claimed over 95% implementation) but that the next phase is specifically to connect front-line/primary health facilities to the internet - i.e. rural clinics are not yet part of the digitised record chain. No evidence found of routine digital data capture at rural clinic point-of-care. Score of 1 stands.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Tunisia record patient data on paper as the default at the point of care. National digitisation efforts, including the unified medical record programme, have concentrated on university and regional hospitals; as of February 2025 the Ministry of Health confirmed that connecting front-line (primary care) facilities to the internet remains a forthcoming phase rather than an achieved one. Research on nursing documentation (2024) similarly finds paper records remain the norm, with electronic nursing records only piloted in a university hospital setting. Telemedicine and rural connectivity initiatives are under development but do not yet substitute for facility-level digital recording in rural clinics.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No evidence found of digital case management systems at rural police stations or gendarmerie posts in Tunisia. Extensive searches reveal digital efforts in cybercrime investigation, forensics training (UNODC), and justice sector digitization (EU/World Bank for courts), but police procedures rely on traditional paper-based processes typical of francophone Africa: handwritten procès-verbaux (PVs) for incidents/complaints, occurrence books ("main courante"), and manual case files. Criminal records (B3) originate from police/gendarmerie stations and involve paper stamps/forms, even if online request portals exist for clean extracts. Rural areas (87% territory covered by National Guard/gendarmerie) lack specific digital pilots; aggregate/central systems absent. US State Dept reports note requirement for "complete record" of arrests/notifications, consistent with paper logs. Score 1: entirely paper-based at facility level.

revision_notes: Original sources (Ministry of Interior homepage, UNODC forensics story, EU justice-digitisation story) were fetched; none directly evidences data-capture status at rural police stations specifically, though they confirm digitisation efforts have concentrated on forensics training and the courts rather than police procedures. A fresh search found no Tunisia-specific study of rural police-station digitisation. A 2020 legal-commentary article confirms Tunisia's justice-sector digital transformation programme (2017-2020) explicitly did not extend electronic data exchange to the police, National Guard, customs or prison services, and that the Code of Criminal Procedure still requires a physical special register for garde-a-vue detentions at police posts. No evidence found of any digital case-management pilot at rural stations specifically. Score of 1 (entirely paper) stands, though the underlying evidence base for rural police specifically remains thinner than for the other facility types.
revised_comments: Rural police stations and National Guard (gendarmerie) posts in Tunisia record incidents, complaints and detentions on paper. The Code of Criminal Procedure requires a physical register for garde-a-vue entries, and Tunisia's justice-sector digitisation programme has historically not extended electronic case exchange to the police, National Guard, customs or prison administration. No evidence of computerised case management, occurrence books or digital procès-verbaux at rural police facilities has been identified; handwritten procès-verbaux and registers remain the standard practice at the point of service.

revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Tunisia (municipal civil status bureaus and their subsidiary offices, annexes and mobile units) record births, deaths and marriages by hand in duplicate paper registers, which hold sole legal probative force. Registrars then manually transcribe these events into the national Madania digital system, giving centralised database access and enabling certificate issuance from any municipal office. A modernisation contract for the Madania platform, financed by the African Development Bank, was signed in March 2021 with the aim of moving toward a more paperless model and improving interoperability with the national ID and other systems, but paper registers remain the primary point-of-service record while this reform is implemented.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Tunisia has implemented national digital platforms like Tarbia.tn (launched under World Bank-supported PREFAT project targeting lagging/rural regions), enabling parents to track real-time attendance, assignments, and progress reports, with teachers managing classes digitally [We Are Tech Africa, World Bank PREFAT]. Equipped 1,600+ computer labs in primary schools, including rural areas, for digital tools. However, no direct evidence of entirely digital recording at rural primary school level for attendance, enrollment, grades; likely paper-based at facilities with aggregation/digital entry at higher levels, given EMIS-like systems common in region but pilots/donor-focused here. Rural infrastructure challenges persist (e.g., poor conditions per reports). Predominantly paper with significant digital pilots/central reporting.

revision_notes: Original sources fetched and confirmed: the Tarbia.tn platform (launched January 2024) provides parents and teachers with a digital portal for attendance, grades and progress tracking, and the World Bank's PREFAT programme (feature published January 2026) confirms consolidation of digital services into tarbia.tn alongside continued infrastructure and teacher-training investment through 2025. A peer-reviewed study of primary-school teachers (Bahloul et al., 2022) found the large majority still do not use technology to produce educational documents and rely on manual/frontal methods, with digital tool use concentrated on browsing and downloading content rather than data entry. No facility-level evidence found that attendance, enrolment or grade data capture at rural primary schools has shifted from paper as the default; digital reporting appears to be populated at classroom or administrative level alongside, rather than replacing, paper record-keeping.
