revised_comments: Tunisia has rolled out national digital education platforms, including Tarbia.tn (launched 2024 under the World Bank-supported PREFAT project targeting lagging and rural regions), giving parents and teachers a portal to track attendance, assignments and progress, and has equipped over 1,600 primary school computer labs, including in rural areas. Digital services have been consolidated into this unified portal as part of the ongoing PREFAT programme through to 2025. Direct data capture at the point of service in rural primary schools, however, continues to rely substantially on manual, paper-based processes, with digital reporting populated at classroom or administrative level rather than replacing paper registers outright, producing a picture of predominantly paper-based recording with significant and growing digital elements.

Comments: In rural Tanzania, birth registration at registry points (Ward Executive Offices and rural health facilities) is predominantly paper-based: registrars complete handwritten forms and issue hand-written certificates on-site.APAI-CRVS Snapshot;Decentralization Study. Digital elements include mobile phone uploads of basic data to RITA's central database post-registration and scanning forms for validation, but initial recording remains manual.APAI-CRVS Snapshot. National digital CRVS launched in 2022 has digitized over 3M records, with eRITA for online applications/certificates, but rural point-of-service unchanged per recent reports.Daily News. Barriers: poor infrastructure, low digital literacy, connectivity issues, reliance on partners for funding/ICT.UNECA Digitalization Report. revision_notes: The APAI-CRVS country snapshot could not be retrieved directly (crawl timeout) but its claims are corroborated by other sources; PMC7595116 (Sanga et al. 2020) and the AfDB/COMESA digitalisation report were fetched and are relevant. Fresh, more specific evidence was found: the Under-Five Birth Registration Initiative (U5BRI), run by RITA with UNICEF/Tigo/Global Affairs Canada support, reached full nationwide rollout across all 26 mainland regions by 8 December 2023. At registration points (health facilities and Ward Executive Offices), registrars complete a two-part hand-written form (registration form plus certificate, issued immediately) while simultaneously using a mobile device/app to upload the same record to RITA's central database in real time (UNECA/GFF issues paper on Rwanda and Tanzania CRVS, 2022; Sanga et al. 2020). This is a genuine hybrid facility-level process - hand-written certificate issuance alongside real-time digital transmission - rather than purely paper capture. Given nationwide coverage of this dual paper/digital model since December 2023, facility-level status is better described as 'Mostly paper - some digital' (code 2) than 'Entirely paper' (code 1). This is a one-step change, not a promotion to the scale ceiling.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry services in Tanzania operate primarily through the Under-Five Birth Registration Initiative, which reached full nationwide coverage across all 26 mainland regions in December 2023. At registration points located in health facilities and Ward Executive Offices, registrars complete a hand-written two-part form - a registration form and an accompanying certificate, issued to the parent immediately - while simultaneously entering the same record via a mobile device or smartphone application that transmits the data to the Registration Insolvency and Trusteeship Agency's central database in real time. Vital events outside this under-five pathway, and district-level processing more broadly, still depend substantially on paper forms that are scanned and archived centrally afterwards. This produces a facility-level pattern of predominantly paper documentation combined with a genuine, real-time digital data channel, rather than a fully paper-based or fully digital process.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Tanzania predominantly use paper-based registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes, which are then aggregated manually into national EMIS systems at district or regional levels. Digital pilots exist, such as InfoTaaluma SMS/app in 253 schools (~4% of secondary schools, unclear primary coverage) and School Information System (SIS) with optional offline/mobile entry proposed in ESDP 2025/30, but these are isolated donor/NGO projects or emerging, not standard at most rural facilities. National EMIS/BEST relies on annual paper forms (TSA) from schools, with rural data gaps due to poor infrastructure, electricity/internet shortages, low digital literacy, and uneven ICT distribution.Tanzania ESDP 2025/30;World Bank SABER. Key barriers: lack of reliable power/internet in rural areas (high cost, sporadic access), inadequate devices/training, teacher workload. National ambitions (ESMIS prototype 2025, digital strategy) outpace rural reality, where paper remains default for point-of-service recording. Score 2 reflects predominant paper with limited digital pilots/aggregation.

revision_notes: Original sources (ESDP 2025/26-2029/30 and the World Bank SDI/SABER survey) were fetched and are relevant, though dated (SDI/SABER survey is from 2019). The Value Code of 1 ('Entirely paper') did not match the accompanying Comments text, which explicitly concluded 'Score 2 reflects predominant paper with limited digital pilots/aggregation' - an internal inconsistency in the original row. Fresh evidence supports code 2: rural primary schools submit official statistics (enrolment, staffing, facilities) via TAMISEMI's Sensa Elimu Msingi online census/EMIS portal, which has replaced the older fully manual reporting process at the point of submission. However, investigative reporting on Mbeya District (Rural Youth Collective survey, August 2025, reported September 2025 and March 2026) finds that day-to-day records - attendance and examination scores - are still taken on paper by teachers and only later entered into EMIS/Sensa Elimu Msingi, frequently by a single self-taught teacher per school (only one in five surveyed schools had any staff member with basic EMIS understanding). The Ministry's Digital National Strategy 2025 confirms partial ICT penetration (61.9% of primary schools grid-connected as of 2023, with 17,700 desktop and 10,384 laptop computers in primary schools nationally) alongside persistent rural connectivity and device gaps. This corroborates the Comments-stated code of 2 rather than the erroneous Value Code of 1.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Tanzania record day-to-day administrative data - attendance registers and examination results - on paper, which teachers complete manually as part of routine practice. Aggregated statistics are subsequently entered into the government's online education data systems, principally TAMISEMI's Sensa Elimu Msingi census portal and the Ministry of Education's EMIS/BEST platform, which have replaced fully manual reporting for annual school censuses. In practice this digital step is often carried out by a single, frequently self-taught, member of staff per school, since formal EMIS training does not reach most rural teachers. Persistent constraints - unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, a shortage of computers, and low digital literacy - mean that most rural schools rely on paper at the point of data capture, with digital systems used mainly for subsequent transmission and aggregation rather than for original recording.

revision_notes: The Kapsuletech blog (a commercial research-services site, not a primary source) claimed GoTHoMIS covers '~71% of dispensaries' with '75% coverage as of 2025', but this figure could not be traced to an official source and is contradicted by primary data. The most authoritative and current source, the Ministry of Health-commissioned Mid-Term Review of HSSP V (Ifakara Health Institute, March 2025), draws on the official Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) 2023 and reports that only 34% of health facilities nationally have computers with internet access, falling to 27% for dispensaries specifically - the facility type that makes up the great majority of rural primary healthcare provision (5,893 of 7,585 total facilities are dispensaries, per University of Dodoma repository data on MoH 2022 figures). GoTHoMIS itself is used by only 10.6% of dispensaries, versus 44.9% of health centres. A further peer-reviewed study (Mwogosi, Discover Public Health / Digital Health, 2025) conducted in Dodoma region found only 41.4% of workstations in rural/dispensary settings had reliable internet, and that rural-based health managers were significantly less likely to use EMR data than urban counterparts (AOR=0.46). Taken together, this evidence indicates rural primary healthcare clinics remain predominantly paper-based at the point of care, with digital capture (chiefly via GoTHoMIS) present but a minority practice nationally - better matching 'Mostly paper - some digital' (code 2) than the original 'Mostly digital - some paper' (code 3). This is a downgrade based on more authoritative, more recent primary survey data (SARA 2023) than the original commercial blog source.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Tanzania - predominantly dispensaries, which account for the large majority of primary-level facilities - remain mostly paper-based in their point-of-care record-keeping. According to the 2023 Service Availability and Readiness Assessment, only 27% of dispensaries have a computer with internet access, and just 10.6% use the Government of Tanzania Health Operations Management Information System (GoTHoMIS), the main electronic medical record platform for primary care; health centres fare somewhat better, at 44.9% GoTHoMIS usage. Where GoTHoMIS or similar systems are in place, workstation and internet reliability remain weak in rural settings, and rural health managers use digital records in decision-making markedly less than their urban counterparts. The result is a facility-level pattern in which paper registers remain the norm for the majority of rural clinics, with digital data capture present at a meaningful but minority share of facilities.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics (HC II/III) in Uganda predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording at point of care, including outpatient/inpatient registers, lab forms, and HMIS tools. Aggregate data from these paper forms is later transcribed into DHIS2 at district level for reporting, leading to errors and delays. Digital systems like EMRs (e.g., UgandaEMR) and DHIS2 are available in higher facilities (HCIV+) but mostly program-specific (HIV), with hybrid paper-digital dominant (94%+ HCIVs); pure digital rare (1-2%). Pilots like Stre@mline exist in select rural hospitals but not scaled nationally. Barriers include unreliable electricity/internet in rural areas (~12% stable connectivity), staff shortages, high turnover, poor ICT infrastructure, and donor-driven silos. National policies (2023-2025 Digital Health Strategy) aim for point-of-care digital by 2025/26, but rural reality lags, with paper default and digital for upward reporting only.

The 2025 cross-sectional BMC study (265 government facilities) confirms 94.3% use a hybrid of paper and electronic records, with only 1.9% purely digital, supporting a 'some digital' element rather than 'entirely paper'. A June 2025 Ministry of Health account confirms EMR rollout (Clinic Master/eAFYA) has reached only 5 Health Centre IVs and 2 Health Centre IIIs nationally as the main programme, but the disease-specific Uganda EMR (HIV/TB) is deployed at 'selected health centre IIs' as ART sites, meaning some rural primary clinics do capture some patient data digitally at point of care. Recalculated from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) since the evidence, read in full, shows a minority digital presence at rural facility level rather than none. Not a top-of-scale promotion so no escalation required.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare facilities (Health Centre II/III) in Uganda continue to rely predominantly on paper-based registers, including outpatient, inpatient, maternity and HMIS tools, for point-of-care data capture. Nationally, 94.3% of surveyed public health facilities operate a hybrid of paper and electronic record systems, with purely digital record-keeping present in only 1.9% of facilities. The Ministry of Health's main Electronic Medical Records rollout (Clinic Master and eAFYA) had, by 2025, reached only 5 Health Centre IVs and 2 Health Centre IIIs nationwide, concentrating instead on national, regional and general hospitals. These initiatives remain confined to specific districts and school networks rather than representing standard practice, so most rural primary schools continue to default to paper-based data capture supplemented by limited digital pilots and periodic digital aggregation.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Zimbabwe primarily use manual paper-based systems for recording criminal cases and complaints, relying on physical dockets prone to loss, tampering, and bribery. Academic studies (e.g., 2019 GIS crime mapping in rural Chivi district) describe traditional crime registers and dockets, with data collected via manual processes and GPS for analysis, indicating no routine digital entry at point of service. ZRP has centralized digital databases (e.g., Criminal Records Office), but rural stations forward paper dockets for processing. Plans for an electronic docket system ("soon" transition announced Dec 2025) and internet provision to rural stations (pledged 2021, per Horizon 2025) remain unimplemented, with no evidence of rural rollout or pilots shifting the norm. Key barriers: poor internet/electricity in rural areas, low device access, resource constraints, as noted in World Bank digital economy report and POTRAZ analyses. National ambitions (e.g., smart policing) contrast sharply with rural paper reality, where digital tools like DMR radios exist for comms but not case recording. Score 1 reflects entirely paper-based point-of-service recording.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Zimbabwe continue to rely on manual paper-based dockets and registers for recording criminal cases and complaints at the point of service. As of December 2025, the Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP) publicly describes a planned transition to an electronic docket management system as still forthcoming ("soon"), confirming that station-level digital case recording has not yet been implemented nationally, let alone in rural areas. A 2021 government pledge to provide internet connectivity to rural police stations to support digitisation remains largely unrealised. Poor rural internet and electricity access, combined with limited device availability, continue to constrain digital adoption at rural stations, while centralised systems such as the Criminal Investigations Department's Interpol-linked databases operate independently of rural point-of-service recording.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Zimbabwe rely entirely on paper-based processes for birth registration, requiring parents to present physical documents such as national ID cards, birth confirmation records (from hospitals/clinics), marriage certificates, baptismal certificates, witness IDs, or letters from village heads/farmers for home/farm births. No evidence found of electronic recording at the point of service in rural facilities; processes emphasize manual declarations and forms. Registration completeness is low in rural areas (~32% in 2015 vs higher urban), with rural residence a key predictor of non-registration alongside poverty, home births, and low maternal education Comparative Population Studies. Nationally, moderate digitization (50-64%) exists for aggregation, but rural point-of-service remains paper due to infrastructure gaps, limited staffing, and indirect costs like transport to district offices UNECA CRVS Report. Recent national digital initiatives (e.g., ZPR integration with health for automated notifications, planned 2023) focus on central systems, starting urban, with mobile apps piloted but no rural rollout confirmed; rural lags persist Biometric Update. Barriers: poor connectivity, economic crisis, under-resourced offices. Gap: National ambitions for e-CRVS contrast with rural paper reality, where data likely transcribed later at district level.

revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Zimbabwe continue to depend on paper-based processes at the point of service, requiring parents and applicants to present physical documents including national identity cards, hospital birth confirmation records, marriage certificates, witness statements, or letters from village heads or farmers for home or farm births. As of mid-2025, the reformed Zimbabwe Population Registry System, which underpins the government's planned digital ID rollout, is being introduced only in Harare and Bulawayo, with extension to the rest of the country not yet under way. Mobile registration drives in remote districts such as Binga rely on temporary outreach teams rather than digitised rural registry offices. National birth registration completeness stood at 57% in the 2023-24 Zimbabwe Demographic and Health Survey, with rural residence remaining a significant predictor of non-registration. Persistent barriers include poor connectivity, under-resourced offices, and the cost and distance involved in reaching district registration centres.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Zimbabwe primarily use paper-based registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Data is collected via annual school census forms filled manually at schools and aggregated upward to the national EMIS, often leading to delays, gaps, and inaccuracies due to manual transcription at district levels. Most rural schools lack digital devices, internet connectivity, and power, preventing real-time digital entry into EMIS; teachers in areas like Mutoko report no access to digital tools for data contribution.Kuyenda Collective EMIS exists nationally, with high continental compliance scores and plans for decentralization, but rural point-of-service remains analog.UNESCO IICBA Pilots like school management software or e-learning platforms (e.g., Ruzivo) target urban/private schools or supplementary use, not routine admin recording in rural public primaries. Key barriers: poor infrastructure (no electricity/internet), teacher ICT skills gaps, funding shortages, high attrition. National policies (e.g., Education 5.0) aspire to digital inclusion, but rural reality lags far behind, with data digitized only post-collection at higher levels. (148 words)

revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Zimbabwe continue to rely on paper-based registers and forms for recording administrative data, attendance and learning outcomes at the point of service. The Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education's annual ED46 school census, most recently updated for 2025, still asks schools to declare whether they maintain digitalised school records, indicating that digital data capture is not standard practice, particularly in under-resourced rural schools lacking computers, electricity and internet connectivity. Plans to merge the Teacher Development Information System with the national Education Management Information System (EMIS) and to decentralise data capture remain in progress rather than realised, and a new school registration information management system commissioned in 2026 is still under development. Rural schools such as those in Mutoko district report no access to digital tools for administrative data entry, with information gathered on paper and transcribed at higher administrative levels.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Zimbabwe traditionally rely on paper registers for patient data recording, with aggregate data later entered into national DHIS2 at district levels. The Impilo EMR system, developed since 2015, is now deployed in 1,254 of ~1,900 public health facilities (66%), explicitly targeting rural 'last mile' sites like Sipepa Rural Hospital through solar power (1,044 facilities, 60% coverage) and internet upgrades to enable digital point-of-care recording. Provincial data (Matabeleland South, Q1 2025) shows 72% fully functional among 153 facilities, though rural districts lag. Digital systems are the emerging standard at most facilities, reducing paper burden and improving patient management, but some paper persists in the remaining ~34% uncovered sites and where infrastructure fails. Key barriers include frequent power outages (costing 6% GDP), poor rural internet/connectivity, training gaps, and staff shortages. National eHealth Strategy (2021-2025) bridges policy ambition with rollout, though rural implementation trails urban areas; majority now predominantly digital with residual paper processes.

revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Zimbabwe are now substantially digitised at the point of care through the Impilo Electronic Health Records system, though paper-based processes persist alongside digital records in a meaningful minority of facilities. As of August 2025, 1,254 of approximately 1,900 public health facilities nationally, around two-thirds, have Impilo deployed, with further expansion under way. Provincial data from the largely rural Matabeleland South province (Q1-Q2 2025) show 90.2% of facilities with EHR infrastructure installed, though only 71.9% fully functional, with rural districts such as Bulilima and Matobo disproportionately affected by unreliable electricity and connectivity; similar patterns are reported in Manicaland province. Zimbabwe's National eHealth Strategy (2021-2025) and continued donor support, including the Global Fund's Digital Health Impact Accelerator, are extending solar power, internet connectivity and digital diagnostic systems to "last mile" rural facilities such as Sipepa Rural Hospital, but frequent power outages, poor rural connectivity and training gaps mean a residual share of rural clinics still rely on paper records.
